title: Taming the Complement Cascade: PNH Midnight Hemolysis, Eculizumab (C5), Pegcetacoplan (C3), Oral Iptacopan (Factor B) & Danicopan (Factor D) — One-Ångström walks inside C5–eculizumab (5I5K), C3c–compstatin (2QKI), Factor B–JGT/iptacopan (6QSW, 6RAV), and self-inhibited Factor D (5NB7); Strübing (1882), Ham (1937), Kinoshita's X-linked PIGA/CD55/CD59 (1993), free-Hb NO/sGC scavenging & Budd-Chiari thrombosis, TRIUMPH & iatrogenic C3 extravascular hemolysis, PEGASUS, APPLY-PNH (NNT 1.25), ALPHA, C5 Arg885His & crovalimab, meningococcal risk math, and 2025–2026 C3G/IgAN breakthroughs

teenKit.tldr: Your immune system has an ancient, hair-trigger defense network called the complement cascade that can accidentally destroy your own red blood cells when molecular armor fails. Modern pharmacology has learned to intercept this atomic destruction using custom-built microscopic wrenches.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding how scientists mapped these proteins down to a single angstrom allows us to turn off friendly-fire biological weapons, transforming once-fatal blood disorders and kidney diseases into manageable conditions.
keyTakeaways: Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH) occurs because a genetic glitch strips red blood cells of their protective shields (CD55 and CD59), leaving them vulnerable to self-destruction.

The complement cascade is a chain reaction where proteins activate one another like dominoes; blocking it too far down can cause new problems, leading scientists to target earlier proteins like Factor B and Factor D.
Structural biologists use atomic-level data (PDB crystal structures) to design precision drugs that physically wedge into proteins and jam their destructive machinery.

vocab.meaning: An ancient network of blood proteins that acts like a hair-trigger alarm system to blast apart invading bacteria, but can accidentally target healthy cells.
A breakthrough antibody drug that binds directly to the C5 protein to block the final, destructive stage of the complement pathway.
An ultra-tiny unit of measurement equal to one ten-billionth of a meter, used by scientists to map individual atoms within proteins.
The premature destruction of red blood cells outside of blood vessels, often happening in the spleen or liver when alternative complement pathways get triggered.

quiz.question: What happens in a patient's body to trigger Paroxysmal Nocturnal Hemoglobinuria (PNH)?
options: Their white blood cells stop producing oxygen.
Mutations wipe out protective surface proteins (CD55 and CD59), exposing red blood cells to friendly-fire attacks.
Their bone marrow completely stops making red blood cells.
An outside virus permanently attaches to hemoglobin and turns it dark brown.
quiz.explanation: PNH is caused by mutations that strip red blood cells of their molecular armor, letting the complement cascade punch holes in them.

quiz.question: Why did scientists develop proximal complement inhibitors like iptacopan (targeting Factor B) after having C5 blockers?
options: C5 blockers were too cheap to manufacture at a commercial scale.
Blocking C5 could sometimes cause trapped red blood cells to be destroyed prematurely elsewhere in the body.
Factor B is located inside the nucleus of white blood cells.
C5 only works against bacteria and has no effect on human cells.
quiz.explanation: While C5 inhibitors stopped cells from bursting in the bloodstream, they sometimes caused a side effect called extravascular hemolysis where cells were cleared in the liver instead, prompting earlier pathway blocks.

quiz.question: How do structural pharmacologists use tools like X-ray crystallography during drug discovery?
options: To track how fast a patient's heart beats during exercise.
To calculate the exact genetic inheritance pattern of rare blood disorders.
To visualize proteins at an atomic scale so they can design exact molecular shapes that jam the protein's function.
To measure the volume of urine a patient produces overnight.
quiz.explanation: Mapping proteins down to the angstrom allows scientists to see exact pockets and shapes where custom-built drug molecules can fit like a key in a lock.
